Salinity in the upper subpolar North Atlantic declined during the 2010s; in other words, the upper waters of the subpolar North Atlantic became less salty over the course of the 2010s. Repeat hydrographic sections, Argo float profiles and moored sensors agreed on the magnitude and the vertical structure of the anomaly, which left its origin to be settled by freshwater budgets and circulation measurements rather than by salinity records alone. The first line of inquiry was the regional freshwater budget. Over recent decades, at least one of two inputs grew, and perhaps both: Greenland meltwater runoff into the North Atlantic increased, and freshwater export from the Arctic through Fram Strait increased. The competing explanation, internal variability of the ocean circulation itself, could be assessed only with sustained transport measurements. The RAPID-MOCHA mooring array has monitored the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation at 26.5°N since 2004, yielding a continuous subtropical transport record against which anomalies could be judged. Subsequently, the OSNAP observing system was deployed across the subpolar North Atlantic in 2014. Interpreting the subpolar records in turn requires close attention to the atmospheric forcing of wintertime mixing. The North Atlantic Oscillation modulates the strength of Labrador Sea convection, and as a result deep convection in the Labrador Sea reached depths of roughly 1,700 metres during the winter of 2014–2015. Such mixing events are the proximate mechanism by which the atmosphere imprints itself on the density structure of the subpolar gyre, and they are therefore the natural place to look for a circulation signature of the freshening. The Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation collapsed completely during the period of observed freshening. The IPCC Sixth Assessment Report concluded that the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation did not collapse during the twentieth and early twenty-first centuries, a finding that cannot be squared with a complete shutdown in those same years. The depth reached by convection in that winter is itself evidence that the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation continued to operate throughout the period of observed freshening; either the circulation collapsed outright in those decades or it went on working through them, exactly one of the two being the case and both together impossible.
